Guided by these insights, we introduce selective fine-tuning of only the final layers responsible for language control. On Qwen-3-32B and Bloom-7.1B, this method achieves over 98 percent language consistency across six languages while fine-tuning only 3-5 percent of parameters, without sacrificing task accuracy. Importantly, this result is nearly identical to that of full-scope fine-tuning (for example, above 98 percent language consistency for both methods across all prompt scenarios) but uses a fraction of the computational resources. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to leverage layer-localization of language control for efficient multilingual adaptation.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Paths Not Taken: Understanding and Mending the Multilingual Factual Recall Pipeline
papers.research_question: Why do multilingual large language models exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, and how can these failures be understood and mended?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a multilingual factual recall pipeline where LLMs use an English-centric mechanism and then translate answers, and introduces two vector interventions to fix errors in translation and recall, significantly improving cross-lingual factual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic insights into the multilingual processing pipeline can be used to design targeted, training-free interventions that direct the model toward better internal paths, unlocking latent multilingual capabilities and improving factual consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs employ a pipeline where factual information is first retrieved in English using intermediate English-centric mechanisms, followed by translation into the target language in later layers.
Two primary failure points cause cross-lingual inconsistencies: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric recall mechanism, and incorrect translation from English back to the target language.
A translation difference vector intervention, derived from the activation difference between explicit translation and fact-recall tasks, steers the model to use more effective translation components, improving conversion correctness.
A recall task vector intervention, extracted from in-context learning examples, promotes the engagement of English-centric factual recall components (like relation propagation and answer extraction) for multilingual prompts.
Combining both interventions leads to substantial improvements in factual recall accuracy, boosting performance by up to 37.6 percentage points for the lowest-performing language and an average gain of 19.04 points across all evaluated languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to five non-English languages and ten relations on a single model (Llama-3.2-3B).
future_direction: Expanding the investigation to more diverse language families and syntactic structures.
Quantifying how the findings apply to relations of varying complexity or different models.
Developing automated methods to identify such weaknesses and implement corresponding solutions.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) often exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, with significantly better performance in factual recall tasks in English than in other languages. The causes of these failures, however, remain poorly understood. Using mechanistic analysis techniques, we uncover the underlying pipeline that LLMs employ, which involves using the English-centric factual recall mechanism to process multilingual queries and then translating English answers back into the target language. We identify two primary sources of error: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric mechanism for factual recall, and incorrect translation from English back into the target language for the final answer. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce two vector interventions, both independent of languages and datasets, to redirect the model toward better internal paths for higher factual consistency. Our interventions combined increase the recall accuracy by over 35 percent for the lowest-performing language. Our findings demonstrate how mechanistic insights can be used to unlock latent multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Cross-model Transferability among Large Language Models on the Platonic Representations of Concepts
papers.research_question: How can conceptual representations (steering vectors) be transferred across different large language models to enable cross-model behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L-Cross Modulation, a linear transformation method to transfer steering vectors across LLMs, demonstrating that conceptual representations are linearly alignable and transferable, even from weaker to stronger models.
papers.conclusion: Cross-model transferability of conceptual representations is achievable via linear transformations, revealing a fundamental universality in how LLMs encode concepts, paving the way for more universal and adaptable language models.
papers.key_findings:
L-Cross Modulation effectively modulates target LLMs using steering vectors transferred from source LLMs.
The linear transformation matrix generalizes across different concepts, enabling alignment of SVs for multiple concepts.
Weak-to-strong transferability: SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively modulate the behavior of larger LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The scope of concepts is limited to eleven benchmark concepts; creating more datasets is resource-intensive.
The evaluation metrics are diverse and may not generalize fully to all concepts.
The hyper-parameter (β) for applying steering vectors is manually tuned rather than automatically optimized.
future_direction: Expand to more high-level concepts with additional datasets.
Develop a unified, comprehensive evaluation framework including a standardized dataset and benchmark.
Automatically determine optimal hyperparameters for applying steering vectors.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical research frontier. Prior research has shown that a single LLM's concept representations can be captured as steering vectors (SVs), enabling the control of LLM behavior (e.g., towards generating harmful content). Our work takes a novel approach by exploring the intricate relationships between concept representations across different LLMs, drawing an intriguing parallel to Plato's Allegory of the Cave. In particular, we introduce a linear transformation method to bridge these representations and present three key findings: 1) Concept representations across different LLMs can be effectively aligned using simple linear transformations, enabling efficient cross-model transfer and behavioral control via SVs. 2) This linear transformation generalizes across concepts, facilitating alignment and control of SVs representing different concepts across LLMs. 3) A weak-to-strong transferability exists between LLM concept representations, whereby SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively control the behavior of larger LLMs.

papers.title: Back Attention: Understanding and Enhancing Multi-Hop Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning, and how can this ability be enhanced?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces back attention, a novel mechanism that allows lower layers to capture higher-layer hidden states, enhancing multi-hop reasoning in LLMs. Also introduces logit flow, an interpretability method for tracing logit propagation.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides new insights into multi-hop reasoning mechanisms and introduces back attention, a powerful and lightweight method that significantly enhances reasoning accuracy in LLMs by allowing lower layers to access higher-layer features.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: entity subject enrichment, entity attribute extraction, relation subject enrichment, and relation attribute extraction.
Finds that failures in multi-hop reasoning often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy.
Proposes back attention, which enables a 1-layer transformer to achieve the performance of a 2-layer transformer on arithmetic tasks.
Back attention, when fine-tuned on a single layer of pre-trained LLMs, significantly improves accuracy across five reasoning datasets and four different models.
Logit flow provides a neuron-level perspective on information flow, offering a more granular understanding than layer-level methods like activation patching.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability analysis primarily focuses on single-hop and two-hop knowledge queries, which represent specific reasoning scenarios; other reasoning tasks might involve different mechanisms.
Back attention is applied to only a single layer in this work, though it could be extended to two or more layers for potentially greater improvements.
future_direction: Extend back attention to two or more layers.
Validate the findings on more diverse reasoning tasks to refine the interpretability framework for broader applicability.
papers.abstract: We investigate how large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning in prompts like "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's mother's spouse is". To analyze this process, we introduce logit flow, an interpretability method that traces how logits propagate across layers and positions toward the final prediction. Using logit flow, we identify four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: (A) entity subject enrichment, (B) entity attribute extraction, (C) relation subject enrichment, and (D) relation attribute extraction. Extending this analysis to multi-hop reasoning, we find that failures often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy. To address this, we propose back attention, a novel mechanism that enables lower layers to leverage higher-layer hidden states from different positions during attention computation. With back attention, a 1-layer transformer achieves the performance of a 2-layer transformer. Applied to four LLMs, back attention improves accuracy on five reasoning datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing latent multi-hop reasoning ability.

papers.title: Analyzing Encoded Concepts in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether transformer language models encode linguistic concepts in their representations, which concepts dominate the overall structure, and whether the models learn novel concepts beyond linguistic properties.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ConceptX, a framework that uses unsupervised clustering to discover latent concepts in transformer language model representations and aligns them with human-defined concepts to explain how linguistic knowledge is structured across layers and models.
papers.conclusion: ConceptX provides a framework for analyzing encoded concepts in deep NLP models, revealing how linguistic information is structured across layers and highlighting differences between models, with many concepts being compositional or novel.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of transformer models predominantly capture shallow lexical concepts (e.g., ngrams, suffixes), while middle and higher layers better represent core linguistic concepts (e.g., morphology, syntax, semantics).
Multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-R) show higher alignment with human-defined concepts compared to monolingual models, likely due to more complex training tasks.
Roughly 50% of the encoded concepts discovered align with the suite of human-defined linguistic concepts; the remaining concepts are novel or compositional, involving multiple fine-grained categories.
The extent of alignment varies across different transformer models and different human-defined concepts, influenced by factors like architecture, training data, and objective function.
Models learn multi-faceted concepts that cannot be adequately explained by existing human-defined concepts, indicating the presence of novel semantic relationships.
papers.limitation:
Clustering a large number of high-dimensional vectors is computationally and memory intensive, requiring the use of a subset of data and limiting the number of tokens per word.
The number of clusters (K=1000) was selected empirically rather than through a rigorous optimization method.
papers.abstract: We propose a novel framework ConceptX, to analyze how latent concepts are encoded in representations learned within pre-trained language models. It uses clustering to discover the encoded concepts and explains them by aligning with a large set of human-defined concepts. Our analysis on seven transformer language models reveal interesting insights: i) the latent space within the learned representations overlap with different linguistic concepts to a varying degree, ii) the lower layers in the model are dominated by lexical concepts (e.g., affixation), whereas the core-linguistic concepts (e.g., morphological or syntactic relations) are better represented in the middle and higher layers, iii) some encoded concepts are multi-faceted and cannot be adequately explained using the existing human-defined concepts.

papers.title: Analogical Reasoning Inside Large Language Models: Concept Vectors and the Limits of Abstraction
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor internal, invariant representations of abstract concepts like those used in analogical reasoning, and how can such representations be extracted and analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Concept Vectors (CVs), distilled from early-to-mid attention heads using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), which provide invariant linear representations for verbal concepts (e.g., antonym) and can causally guide model behavior. It finds that abstract concepts like 'previous' and 'next' lack such invariant representations, limiting generalization.
papers.conclusion: While LLMs form invariant linear representations (CVs) for verbal concepts, they lack such representations for more abstract relational concepts like 'previous' and 'next', which hinders their ability to generalize analogical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Function Vectors (FVs) are not invariant to low-level input changes (e.g., open-ended vs. multiple-choice format) and encode multiple task attributes beyond the latent concept.
Activation patching, used to identify FVs, localizes components causally important for output but fails to identify heads encoding latent conceptual information.
Concept Vectors (CVs) for verbal concepts are invariant to low-level transformations and emerge in early-to-mid layers, acting as feature detectors that can represent the correct concept even when the model's final output is incorrect.
CVs can causally guide model behavior in-context and are more portable across low-level task variations than FVs, though FVs are more effective in zero-shot settings.
Abstract concepts like 'previous' and 'next' do not form invariant linear representations in the models studied, which correlates with poor generalization on tasks requiring abstraction, such as letter-string analogies.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses exclusively on linear representations, despite evidence that LLM representations can be nonlinear, potentially missing nonlinear encodings of abstract concepts.
Conclusions are restricted to the Llama-3.1 8B and 70B models, leaving generalizability to other architectures untested.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning relies on conceptual abstractions, but it is unclear whether Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor such internal representations. We explore distilled representations from LLM activations and find that function vectors (FVs; Todd et al., 2024) - compact representations for in-context learning (ICL) tasks - are not invariant to simple input changes (e.g., open-ended vs. multiple-choice), suggesting they capture more than pure concepts. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), we localize a small set of attention heads that encode invariant concept vectors (CVs) for verbal concepts like "antonym". These CVs function as feature detectors that operate independently of the final output - meaning that a model may form a correct internal representation yet still produce an incorrect output. Furthermore, CVs can be used to causally guide model behaviour. However, for more abstract concepts like "previous" and "next", we do not observe invariant linear representations, a finding we link to generalizability issues LLMs display within these domains.

papers.title: Demystifying the Roles of LLM Layers in Retrieval, Knowledge, and Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the contribution of each layer to overall LLM performance under different evaluation protocols?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematically shows that depth usage in LLMs is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent, with shallow layers dominating likelihood and retrieval tasks, while middle and deeper layers are crucial for reasoning and generation.
papers.conclusion: Results show that layer contributions are highly uneven: shallow layers dominate likelihood and retrieval, while mid-to-deep layers are essential for reasoning and generation. Depth usage is inherently task-dependent, highly metric-sensitive, and strongly model-specific, highlighting the critical need for task-aware evaluation and offering practical guidance for compression and future model design.
papers.key_findings:
Under likelihood-based metrics, pruning most layers preserves performance, with only initial layers being critical; generation-based evaluation shows middle and deeper layers are indispensable for reasoning and long-range coherence.
Knowledge and retrieval are concentrated in shallow components, with removal of early layers causing sharp degradation in retrieval tasks.
Reasoning accuracy relies heavily on deeper layers and is more sensitive to ablation in middle and deep layers.
Distillation not only improves baseline accuracy but also redistributes reasoning capacity more evenly across depth, enhancing robustness under ablation.
Retrieval and reasoning abilities are localized to specific attention heads rather than being uniformly distributed.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that the deeper layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) contribute little to representation learning and can often be removed without significant performance loss. However, such claims are typically drawn from narrow evaluations and may overlook important aspects of model behavior. In this work, we present a systematic study of depth utilization across diverse dimensions, including evaluation protocols, task categories, and model architectures. Our analysis confirms that very deep layers are generally less effective than earlier ones, but their contributions vary substantially with the evaluation setting. Under likelihood-based metrics without generation, pruning most layers preserves performance, with only the initial few being critical. By contrast, generation-based evaluation uncovers indispensable roles for middle and deeper layers in enabling reasoning and maintaining long-range coherence. We further find that knowledge and retrieval are concentrated in shallow components, whereas reasoning accuracy relies heavily on deeper layers -- yet can be reshaped through distillation. These results highlight that depth usage in LLMs is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent, underscoring the need for task-, metric-, and model-aware perspectives in both interpreting and compressing large models.

papers.title: Lens: Rethinking Multilingual Enhancement for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the multilingual capabilities of English-centric large language models efficiently without causing catastrophic forgetting of English and off-target issues?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes LENS, a method that enhances multilingual capabilities by leveraging internal language representation spaces, achieving better performance with less computational cost and without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: LENS is an effective, efficient, and scalable method for multilingual enhancement of large language models.
papers.key_findings:
LENS improves multilingual performance while maintaining English proficiency.
LENS requires less computational cost compared to existing post-training approaches.
Separating language representations in language-specific subspaces is crucial for multilingual performance.
Aligning multiple languages in language-agnostic subspaces primarily enhances multilingual comprehension.
Maintaining stable representations of the central language provides reliable alignment supervision.
future_direction: Combining the LENS training paradigm with advancements in data selection and filtering methods.
papers.abstract: As global demand for multilingual large language models (LLMs) grows, most LLMs still remain overly focused on English, leading to the limited access to advanced AI for non-English speakers. Current methods to enhance multilingual capabilities largely rely on data-driven post-training techniques, such as multilingual instruction tuning or continual pre-training. However, these approaches exhibit significant limitations, including high resource cost, exacerbation of off-target issue and catastrophic forgetting of central language abilities. To this end, we propose Lens, a novel approach that enhances multilingual capabilities by leveraging LLMs' internal language representation spaces. Lens operates on two subspaces: the language-agnostic subspace, where it aligns target languages with the central language to inherit strong semantic representations, and the language-specific subspace, where it separates target and central languages to preserve linguistic specificity. Experiments on three English-centric LLMs show that Lens significantly improves multilingual performance while maintaining the model's English proficiency, achieving better results with less computational cost compared to existing post-training approaches.

papers.title: Probing LLMs for Joint Encoding of Linguistic Categories
papers.research_question: How are linguistically related syntactic categories jointly encoded in LLMs, and do these patterns hold across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence that linguistically related syntactic categories are jointly encoded in LLMs, with similar patterns across languages and between different levels of the linguistic hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs, supporting the idea that models learn hierarchical and shared representations for syntax across languages.
papers.key_findings:
POS tags that are linguistically related are jointly encoded in both monolingual and multilingual models.
Joint encoding patterns are consistent across English, Italian, and Greek in multilingual models.
Information about linguistic categories can be shared across languages, indicating language-agnostic encoding.
There is evidence of joint encoding between POS tags and dependency relations, suggesting information sharing across tasks.
The cross-neutralization method effectively reveals shared representations without tuning the base models.
papers.limitation:
Limited to encoder-only architectures.
Only three languages are examined.
Limited to syntactic tasks (POS tagging and dependency labeling).
Lack of cross-neutralization effects does not necessarily indicate absence of joint encoding.
future_direction: Extend experiments to more languages, particularly low-resource and typologically distant languages.
Include higher-level semantic tasks such as semantic role labeling and coreference resolution.
Explore other model architectures like encoder-decoder or decoder-only models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance on a range of NLP tasks, due to the general-purpose linguistic knowledge acquired during pretraining. Existing model interpretability research (Tenney et al., 2019) suggests that a linguistic hierarchy emerges in the LLM layers, with lower layers better suited to solving syntactic tasks and higher layers employed for semantic processing. Yet, little is known about how encodings of different linguistic phenomena interact within the models and to what extent processing of linguistically-related categories relies on the same, shared model representations. In this paper, we propose a framework for testing the joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs. Focusing on syntax, we find evidence of joint encoding both at the same (related part-of-speech (POS) classes) and different (POS classes and related syntactic dependency relations) levels of linguistic hierarchy. Our cross-lingual experiments show that the same patterns hold across languages in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Revealing emergent human-like conceptual representations from language prediction
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) develop human-like concepts through language prediction, and how such concepts are represented, organized, and linked to behavior.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge in LLMs purely from language prediction, without real-world grounding. These representations converge to a shared, context-independent structure that predicts model performance and aligns with human behavioral and neural data.
papers.conclusion: The findings establish that critical aspects of human conceptual representation and organization can emerge purely from language prediction in LLMs, offering a tractable window into human concepts and advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from definitional descriptions using in-context learning, with performance improving with more demonstrations.
The conceptual representations formed by LLMs converge toward a shared, context-independent relational structure as the number of contextual demonstrations increases.
Alignment of a model's conceptual representations with this convergent structure reliably predicts its performance on a range of language understanding and reasoning tasks.
LLM-derived conceptual representations effectively predict human behavioral judgments, such as similarity ratings and categorization, outperforming static word embeddings.
The convergent conceptual representations align closely with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for their biological plausibility.
papers.limitation: LLMs struggled to predict human judgments when they relied on perceptual properties like color or texture, indicating a divergence from human judgments in visually grounded dimensions.
papers.abstract: People acquire concepts through rich physical and social experiences and use them to understand and navigate the world. In contrast, large language models (LLMs), trained solely through next-token prediction on text, exhibit strikingly human-like behaviors. Are these models developing concepts akin to those of humans? If so, how are such concepts represented, organized, and related to behavior? Here, we address these questions by investigating the representations formed by LLMs during an in-context concept inference task. We found that LLMs can flexibly derive concepts from linguistic descriptions in relation to contextual cues about other concepts. The derived representations converge toward a shared, context-independent structure, and alignment with this structure reliably predicts model performance across various understanding and reasoning tasks. Moreover, the convergent representations effectively capture human behavioral judgments and closely align with neural activity patterns in the human brain, providing evidence for biological plausibility. Together, these findings establish that structured, human-like conceptual representations can emerge purely from language prediction without real-world grounding, highlighting the role of conceptual structure in understanding intelligent behavior. More broadly, our work suggests that LLMs offer a tangible window into the nature of human concepts and lays the groundwork for advancing alignment between artificial and human intelligence.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Language Mixing in Reasoning Language Models: Patterns, Impact, and Internal Causes
papers.research_question: What are the patterns, performance impact, and internal causes of language mixing (reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt) in Reasoning Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of language mixing in Reasoning Language Models, showing it reflects latent internal processing preferences (a bias towards Latin and Han scripts) and that controlling the reasoning script via constrained decoding can significantly improve multilingual reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Language mixing in RLMs is a systematic behavior tied to the models' internal language preferences; controlling the reasoning script based on these preferences offers a practical way to optimize multilingual reasoning performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Language mixing is most prevalent when the input language is neither English nor Chinese, suggesting these serve as internal pivot languages.
The degree of language mixing increases with task difficulty and is more pronounced in STEM subjects.
Distillation amplifies language mixing compared to the base backbone models.
Forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy for non-Latin/Han-script input languages.
The script composition of reasoning traces closely mirrors that of the model's internal representations (analyzed via Logit Lens), indicating language mixing reflects latent processing preferences.
papers.limitation: Analysis focuses on valid reasoning traces that conclude with a final answer, excluding cases of endless reasoning.
future_direction: Controlling and adapting the reasoning language to build more robust, interpretable, and user-aligned RLMs.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models (RLMs) excel at complex tasks by leveraging a chain-of-thought process to generate structured intermediate steps. However, language mixing, i.e., reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt, has been observed in their outputs and shown to affect performance, though its impact remains debated. We present the first systematic study of language mixing in RLMs, examining its patterns, impact, and internal causes across 15 languages, 7 task difficulty levels, and 18 subject areas, and show how all three factors influence language mixing. Moreover, we demonstrate that the choice of reasoning language significantly affects performance: forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy. Finally, we show that the script composition of reasoning traces closely aligns with that of the model's internal representations, indicating that language mixing reflects latent processing preferences in RLMs. Our findings provide actionable insights for optimizing multilingual reasoning and open new directions for controlling reasoning languages to build more interpretable and adaptable RLMs.

papers.title: First Align, then Predict: Understanding the Cross-Lingual Ability of Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What parts of the model and what mechanisms support zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual BERT?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT operates as the stacking of two modules: a multilingual encoder in the lower layers critical for cross-lingual transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little importance for transfer.
papers.conclusion: mBERT is constructed from a multilingual encoder in the lower layers that aligns representations across languages and is critical for cross-language transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little effect on transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of mBERT are critical for cross-lingual transfer, while upper layers are task-specific and language-agnostic.
Cross-lingual similarity (CKA) between representations of source and target languages is highest in the middle layers and strongly correlates with cross-lingual performance.
Randomly initializing lower layers harms cross-lingual performance but not same-language performance, indicating their specific role in cross-lingual alignment.
The cross-lingual alignment learned during pretraining is preserved after fine-tuning.
This mechanism suggests mBERT reproduces the standard cross-lingual pipeline without explicit supervision.
future_direction: Using the findings to design better multilingual pre-training processes.
Inspecting the mismatch with Singh et al. (2019) who found no language alignment across layers for Natural Language Inference.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot crosslingual transfer capabilities. Such transfer emerges by fine-tuning on a task of interest in one language and evaluating on a distinct language, not seen during the fine-tuning. Despite promising results, we still lack a proper understanding of the source of this transfer. Using a novel layer ablation technique and analyses of the model's internal representations, we show that multilingual BERT, a popular multilingual language model, can be viewed as the stacking of two sub-networks: a multilingual encoder followed by a taskspecific language-agnostic predictor. While the encoder is crucial for cross-lingual transfer and remains mostly unchanged during finetuning, the task predictor has little importance on the transfer and can be reinitialized during fine-tuning. We present extensive experiments with three distinct tasks, seventeen typologically diverse languages and multiple domains to support our hypothesis.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Explainability and Interpretability of Multilingual Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.research_question: What are the current explainability and interpretability methods for multilingual large language models, and what are the key challenges and future directions in this domain?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first comprehensive survey of explainability and interpretability methods for multilingual large language models, categorizing existing literature and outlining key challenges and future research avenues.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes research on MLLM explainability, identifies key challenges like the focus on high-resource languages, and outlines future directions for advancing multilingual interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Research on low-resource languages remains underrepresented in MLLM explainability studies.
Existing explainability techniques are often applied to multilingual contexts without significant methodological innovations.
There is a need to expand beyond linguistic case studies to areas such as cultural values, regional variations, and language bias.
The exploration of language-agnostic latent spaces is a promising trend for understanding cross-lingual capabilities.
Explanation faithfulness is a critical challenge, especially for token-based attributions in complex multilingual tasks.
future_direction: Developing novel multilingual explainability innovations dedicated to multilingual contexts.
Advancing work on language-specific features and extra-language knowledge such as cultural values and regional variations.
Improving explainability research for low-resource languages by shifting focus to core NLP tasks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) demonstrate state-of-the-art capabilities across diverse cross-lingual and multilingual tasks. Their complex internal mechanisms, however, often lack transparency, posing significant challenges in elucidating their internal processing of multilingualism, cross-lingual transfer dynamics and handling of language-specific features. This paper addresses this critical gap by presenting a survey of current explainability and interpretability methods specifically for MLLMs. To our knowledge, it is the first comprehensive review of its kind. Existing literature is categorised according to the explainability techniques employed, the multilingual tasks addressed, the languages investigated and available resources. The survey further identifies key challenges, distils core findings and outlines promising avenues for future research within this rapidly evolving domain.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Hyperpolyglot LLMs: Cross-Lingual Interpretability in Token Embeddings
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models (LLMs) represent relationships between languages in their input token embeddings? Specifically, does the geometry of these embeddings encode language identity or cross-lingual semantic similarity?
papers.core_contribution: The geometry of input token embeddings in multilingual LLMs is interpretable and differs between model families: XLM-RoBERTa embeddings encode language identity (writing systems), while mT5 embeddings encode cross-lingual semantic similarity without explicit parallel training.
papers.conclusion: Input token embeddings of LLMs are interpretable and meaningful, and mT5 accidentally achieves cross-lingual semantic alignment without explicit supervision, a goal that previously required dedicated methods.
papers.key_findings:
XLM-RoBERTa token embeddings linearly separate writing systems with 99.2% accuracy.
mT5 token embeddings have nearest neighbors that are often translations, with an average of 7.61 writing systems in the top 50 neighbors.
The geometry of token embeddings is consistent across parameter scales within the same model family.
mT5 discovers a shared cross-lingual semantic space without explicit parallel data or training objective.
The patterns in token embeddings are interpretable and differ by model family.
papers.limitation: The work is descriptive rather than explanatory; it observes patterns but cannot identify causal factors due to the many differences in model architectures, training methods, and pre-training corpora between LLM families.
future_direction: Explaining factors causing the different token embedding patterns (model architectures, pre-training procedures, data curation).
Exploring the utility of combining low-resource languages with closely related higher-resource languages in pre-training corpora.
Exploring potential applications of cross-lingual representations embedded in LLMs for downstream tasks and model selection.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer learning is an important property of multilingual large language models (LLMs). But how do LLMs represent relationships between languages? Every language model has an input layer that maps tokens to vectors. This ubiquitous layer of language models is often overlooked. We find that similarities between these input embeddings are highly interpretable and that the geometry of these embeddings differs between model families. In one case (XLM-RoBERTa), embeddings encode language: tokens in different writing systems can be linearly separated with an average of 99.2% accuracy. Another family (mT5) represents cross-lingual semantic similarity: the 50 nearest neighbors for any token represent an average of 7.61 writing systems, and are frequently translations. This result is surprising given that there is no explicit parallel cross-lingual training corpora and no explicit incentive for translations in pre-training objectives. Our research opens the door for investigations in 1) The effect of pre-training and model architectures on representations of languages and 2) The applications of cross-lingual representations embedded in language models.

papers.title: Mitigating Negative Interference in Multilingual Knowledge Editing through Null-Space Constraints
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently update knowledge in multilingual large language models sequentially across languages without causing negative interference and while preserving multilingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LangEdit, a null-space constrained framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that projects parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: LangEdit is an effective framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that uses null-space projection to isolate language-specific updates, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization, as demonstrated across multiple models and languages.
papers.key_findings:
LangEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance in multilingual sequential knowledge editing, improving editing accuracy and multilingual generalization across three model architectures and six languages.
LangEdit effectively mitigates negative interference by projecting language-specific updates onto the null space of previous updates, preserving performance in previously edited languages.
The method demonstrates cross-lingual knowledge transfer, where edits in one language can be accessed in another without explicit editing in that language.
Editing effectiveness varies by language, with languages having less pretraining data (e.g., Spanish) showing greater improvement than high-resource languages (e.g., English).
LangEdit maintains high specificity, ensuring that edits do not affect unrelated knowledge, and improves downstream task performance on multilingual benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on 6-8B parameter LLMs; extending to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) could reveal scaling effects.
The current evaluation focuses on constrained editing scenarios; future work should explore a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Multilingual experiments are limited to 6 languages; developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages would better test the boundaries of LangEdit and baselines.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) to reveal scaling effects.
Exploring a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages.
papers.abstract: Efficiently updating multilingual knowledge in large language models (LLMs), while preserving consistent factual representations across languages, remains a long-standing and unresolved challenge.While deploying separate editing systems for each language might seem viable, this approach incurs substantial costs due to the need to manage multiple models.A more efficient solution involves integrating knowledge updates across all languages into a unified model.However, performing sequential edits across languages often leads to destructive parameter interference, significantly degrading multilingual generalization and the accuracy of injected knowledge.To address this challenge, we propose LangEdit, a novel null-space constrained framework designed to precisely isolate language-specific knowledge updates.The core innovation of LangEdit lies in its ability to project parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces.This approach mathematically guarantees update independence while preserving multilingual generalization capabilities.We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across three model architectures, six languages, and four downstream tasks, demonstrating that LangEdit effectively mitigates parameter interference and outperforms existing state-of-the-art editing methods.Our results highlight its potential for enabling efficient and accurate multilingual knowledge updates in LLMs.The code is available at https: //github.com/VRCMF/LangEdit.git.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.research_question: Can editing representations, instead of weights, be a more powerful alternative for parameter-efficient finetuning of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representation Finetuning (ReFT), a family of parameter-efficient finetuning methods that edit hidden representations instead of weights, and shows that it is more parameter-efficient and often outperforms existing PEFTs.
papers.conclusion: ReFT methods are a promising alternative to weight-based PEFTs, offering a better balance of efficiency and performance, and are worthy of further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
ReFT methods are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
LoReFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on commonsense reasoning, instruction-following, and natural language understanding.
ReFT methods are less effective on arithmetic reasoning tasks, possibly due to the length of chain-of-thought generations.
ReFT performance scales with model size.
LoReFT outperforms full finetuning on instruction-following with only 0.0039% of parameters.
papers.limitation: ReFTs may have trouble with chain-of-thought reasoning tasks due to the length of generations and overall greater difficulty of the task.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks, instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Distributional reasoning in LLMs: Parallel reasoning processes in multi-hop reasoning
papers.research_question: What strategy does an LLM use to solve multi-hop reasoning questions when not explicitly writing down a thought process (i.e., without chain-of-thought)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that during multi-hop reasoning, LLMs internally activate a distribution of potential intermediate answers in middle layers, and the final answer can be approximated via a linear transformation from this distribution, revealing parallel reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a distributional reasoning process for multi-hop questions, characterized by parallel activation of intermediate possibilities and a linear transformation to final answers, bridging associative and propositional reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The activation vector of potential final answers (A2) can be linearly approximated from the activation vector of potential intermediate answers (A1) extracted from middle layers, with R^2 > 0.5 on average.
Middle layers generate highly interpretable embeddings representing a set of potential intermediate answers, followed by a phase transition where A1 activations decrease and A2 activations increase.
High Spearman correlation exists between the order of top-activated A1 logits in middle layers and their corresponding A2 logits in the output layer.
The same distributional reasoning process occurs even when the model hallucinates answers (on fictitious subjects or out-of-distribution attributes).
The reasoning process is largely handled at the final token position after the middle layers, with minimal influence from other token positions.
papers.limitation:
The questions have a similar general structure; altering the structure could lead to different results.
Different prompt structures, question types, or subjects could lead the model to employ various solving strategies.
The analysis cannot account for semantic categories that lack clear representative tokens (e.g., years).
The statistical analyses do not show direct causality.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for semantic categories lacking clear representative tokens.
Investigate direct causality in the observed process.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to perform tasks believed to require thought processes. When the model does not document an explicit thought process, it becomes difficult to understand the processes occurring within its hidden layers and to determine if these processes can be referred to as reasoning. We introduce a novel and interpretable analysis of internal multi-hop reasoning processes in LLMs. We demonstrate that the prediction process for compositional reasoning questions can be modeled using a simple linear transformation between two semantic category spaces. We show that during inference, the middle layers of the network generate highly interpretable embeddings that represent a set of potential intermediate answers for the multi-hop question. We use statistical analyses to show that a corresponding subset of tokens is activated in the model's output, implying the existence of parallel reasoning paths. These observations hold true even when the model lacks the necessary knowledge to solve the task. Our findings can help uncover the strategies that LLMs use to solve reasoning tasks, offering insights into the types of thought processes that can emerge from artificial intelligence. Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization.
